ety.text: From Middle English nou, nu, from Old English nū, from Proto-West Germanic *nū, from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”). Doublet of nu ("well?"). Cognates Cognate with Scots noo, nou, now (“now”), Yola neow, now, nowe (“now”), North Frisian nü (“now”), West Frisian no (“now”), Dutch nu, nou (“now”), German nu, nun (“now”), Limburgish noe, Nuu (“now”), Danish and Swedish nu (“now”), Elfdalian nų (“now”), Faroese nú, núgv (“now”), Icelandic nú, núna (“now”), Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk no, nu, nå (“now”), Gothic 𐌽𐌿 (nu, “now”); also Gaulish nu (“now”), La…

senses.d: Present; current.
ex: Defects seem as necessary to our now happiness as their Opposites.

senses.d: Fashionable; popular; up to date; current.
ex: I think this band's sound is very now.

Bernard: What does it do?
Fran: It's very in.
Bernard: You don't know what it is, do you?
Fran: It's very now.

senses.d: At the present time.
ex: Now I am six.
Stop that now, Jimmy!

senses.d: Used to introduce a point, a qualification of what has previously been said, a remonstration or a rebuke.
ex: Now, we all want what is best for our children.
Now, Jimmy, stop that.

senses.d: Differently from the immediate past; differently from a more remote past or a possible future; differently from all other times.
ex: Now I am ready.
We all now want the latest toys for our children.

senses.d: At the time reached within a narration.
ex: Now he remembered why he had come.
He now asked her whether she had made pudding.

senses.d: Used to indicate a context of urgency.
ex: Now listen, we must do something about this.

senses.d: At the present point of a recurring cycle or event.
ex: I always used to do my shopping now, to avoid the rush.

senses.d: Very recently; not long ago; up to the present.
ex: They that but now, for honour and for plate, / Made the sea blush with blood, resign their hate.

senses.d: Used to address a switching side, or sharp change in attitude from before.
ex: Now, you want to protect me. An hour ago, you were mercilessly bullying me!

senses.d: Sometimes; occasionally; used to list a series of often assumed states.
ex: His face fit his roles: now smiling, now earnest, now glowering, now raging.

senses.d: Since, because, in light of the fact.
ex: Now all the children have grown up and left, the house is very quiet.
Now that my sister has gotten rid of their cat, we can go to her house this coming Thanksgiving.

senses.d: Indicates a signal to begin.
ex: Now! Fire all we've got while the enemy is in reach!

senses.d: The present time.
ex: Now is the right time.
There is no better time than now.

senses.d: The state of not paying attention to the future or the past.
ex: She is living in the now.

senses.d: A particular instant in time, as perceived at that instant.
ex: Forever is composed of Nows— / 'T is not a different time, / Except for infiniteness / And latitude of home.

grp.label: occasionally; used to list a series of often assumed states

ety.text: Inherited from Old French maintenant.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addessum. Documented since the late thirteenth century.
Derived from Latin hōrā, ablative case of hōra (“hour”). Compare Old French ore, Spanish ahora and Portuguese agora.

Ancient Greek ὥρᾱ (hṓrā)bor. Latin hōrā Old Spanish agora Spanish ahora Inherited from Old Spanish agora, from Latin hāc hōrā (“at this time”). pt:agora.gl: now; right now (at the present time)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese agora, from Latin hāc hōrā. Compare Galician agora and Spanish ahora. To a lesser extent, compare also Italian ora and Old French ore.

Inherited from Middle French alors, from Old French alors, a leurs, allors, alores, alour, alore, alora (also as enlor, enlora, etc.), from Old French a + lors. Compare Italian allora, Spanish alora, Occitan alara and Catalan aleshores.
From Middle French ore, from Old French ore, from Vulgar Latin hā horā, alteration of hāc horā (“(in) this hour”, ablative). Compare Italian ora, Spanish ahora, Portuguese agora.

fr:tantôt.gl: soon, shortly (used with the present tense)

ety.text: From tant + tôt.
Cognate with Spanish ya que and Italian giacché.
Inherited from Old Spanish ya (“already; now”), from Latin iam. Compare Ladino ya, Asturian yá, Galician xa, Portuguese já, Catalan ja, French déjà, and Italian già.

pt:já.gl: already (indicating that something has happened before)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese ja, from Latin iam (“already”). Compare Spanish ya.

phr: even a blind squirrel finds an acorn every now and then

ety.text: From Middle English nowher, from Old English nōhwēr, nāhwǣr, from nā- + hwǣr. By surface analysis, no + where. Adjective usage is taken from phrases like nowhere on the map (signifying the location was too small or too insignificant to be listed), nowhere you want to be, etc.

senses.d: In no place.
ex: Nowhere did the rules say anything about popcorn.
The keys are nowhere in the house.

senses.d: To no place.
ex: We sat in traffic, going nowhere.
If you forget to do this, your interlock circuit won't be made and you'll be going nowhere.

senses.d: Unimportant; unworthy of notice.
ex: Elinore was such a bitch, such a nowhere person.

senses.d: No particular place, noplace.
ex: They went on a cruise to nowhere.
On a warm summer's evening On a train bound for nowhere I met up with the gambler

ety.text: From now + adays.

senses.d: At the present time; in the current era.
ex: Cars nowadays are more efficient.
What is it that now adayes makes all our quarrells mortall?

grp.label: at the present time; in the current era

ety.text: From actuel + -ment.
Inherited from Middle French auiourd'huy; univerbation of au + jour + de + hui, literally “on the day of today”; since hui comes from Latin hodie.
From oggi + dì.
From oggi (“today”) + giorno (“day”).

es:hoy en día.gl: nowadays; these days; in the present time or era

ety.text: Inherited from Latin hōc annō, ablative of hic + annus (“this year”). Compare Portuguese ogano and Asturian anguaño.
Literally, “today in day”. Compare Spanish hoy en día and Catalan avui en dia.

From Old Galician-Portuguese oge (“today”), from Latin hodiē (“today”), from hōc (“this”) + diē (“day”). Cognate with Galician hoxe, Spanish hoy, Catalan avui, French hui and Italian oggi.
